title: Chronic hepatitis B (adult)
subject: gastroenterology
summary: Assess every HBsAg-positive adult with ALT, HBV DNA, APRI or elastography and coinfection tests. WHO 2024 expands treatment to anyone with significant fibrosis, HBV DNA above 2000 IU/mL with raised ALT, or key risk conditions, using tenofovir disoproxil or entecavir long term. Give tenofovir in pregnancy when HBV DNA is 200,000 IU/mL or more.

sections.title: Recognise and assess
items: Chronic infection: HBsAg positive (persisting 6 months or more). Test HBeAg and anti-HBe, HBV DNA (quantitative), ALT, AST, full blood count, creatinine, and APRI or transient elastography.
ALT upper limit of normal (WHO 2024): 30 U/L for men and 19 U/L for women. ALT fluctuates, so decisions use at least two values over 6 to 12 months.
Significant fibrosis (F2): APRI above 0.5 or elastography above 7 kPa. Cirrhosis (F4): clinical features, APRI above 1, or elastography above 12.5 kPa (FibroScan cut-offs).
Test all HBsAg-positive people for HIV, hepatitis C and hepatitis D (anti-HDV, then HDV RNA if positive). Low HBV DNA with high ALT should raise suspicion of HDV.
Ask about family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis, alcohol, diabetes, fatty liver, and planned immunosuppression or chemotherapy.

sections.title: Who to treat (WHO 2024)
items: Treat any adult or adolescent (12 years or older) with significant fibrosis or cirrhosis (APRI above 0.5 or elastography above 7 kPa, or cirrhosis), regardless of HBV DNA or ALT.
OR HBV DNA above 2000 IU/mL with ALT above the upper limit of normal.

OR regardless of fibrosis, HBV DNA or ALT: coinfection (HIV, HDV or HCV), family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis, immune suppression (long-term steroids, transplant), diabetes or MASLD, or extrahepatic manifestations (glomerulonephritis, vasculitis).
OR, where HBV DNA testing is unavailable: persistently abnormal ALT (two values above normal over 6 to 12 months), regardless of APRI.
Decompensated cirrhosis (ascites, variceal bleeding, encephalopathy, jaundice): start antiviral therapy immediately and refer for transplant assessment.

AASLD/IDSA 2025 is similar in spirit: treatment is conditionally advised in the immune-tolerant phase if over 40 or with F2 or more fibrosis, and offered by shared decision in the indeterminate phase.

sections.title: What to use
items: Preferred: tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or entecavir (ETV), both with a high barrier to resistance.
Use entecavir or tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) for established osteoporosis or impaired kidney function. TAF is not recommended if eGFR is below 15 mL/min.
Where TDF alone is not available, TDF plus lamivudine or TDF plus emtricitabine are acceptable alternatives. Do not use lamivudine, adefovir or telbivudine monotherapy (resistance).
Entecavir is not recommended after lamivudine resistance; switch to tenofovir for suspected resistance or treatment failure (reinforce adherence first).
Therapy is usually lifelong. Never stop in cirrhosis. Stopping is considered only in specialist care (e.g. after HBsAg loss) with close follow-up for flares.

sections.title: Pregnancy and mother-to-child transmission
items: Test every pregnant woman for HBsAg as early as possible in each pregnancy.

HBsAg positive with HBV DNA 200,000 IU/mL or more (or HBeAg positive): tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg daily, preferably from the second trimester (WHO; AASLD/IDSA 2025: start by week 28), until at least delivery or completion of the infant vaccine series.
Where neither HBV DNA nor HBeAg testing is available, WHO 2024 advises tenofovir prophylaxis for all HBsAg-positive pregnant women.
Assess the mother for long-term treatment eligibility, but do not delay prophylaxis. ALT may normalise in pregnancy, so reassess after delivery; watch for postpartum flares if tenofovir is stopped.

Infant: hepatitis B vaccine birth dose as soon as possible (within 24 hours), plus hepatitis B immunoglobulin within 12 hours of birth where available, then complete the vaccine series. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: On treatment: at least annually ALT, AST, HBV DNA, HBsAg, HBeAg and anti-HBe, and APRI or elastography; every 3 to 6 months in the first year, in cirrhosis, HIV coinfection, renal impairment or poor adherence. Check adherence at every visit.
TDF: baseline and annual creatinine and eGFR (more often if risk factors such as age over 60, eGFR below 50, diabetes, hypertension, nephrotoxic drugs).
Not yet eligible for treatment: monitor ALT and HBV DNA at least annually and reassess eligibility.
HCC surveillance with ultrasound and AFP every 6 months: all with cirrhosis, those with a family history of HCC, and (WHO) people over 40 with HBV DNA above 20,000 IU/mL even without cirrhosis.

sections.title: Prevention and reactivation
items: Test and vaccinate household and sexual contacts; advise against sharing razors or toothbrushes.

Before chemotherapy, anti-CD20 therapy, other potent immunosuppression or HCV direct-acting antivirals, test HBsAg and anti-HBc. HBsAg-positive patients need antiviral prophylaxis (entecavir or tenofovir) and specialist input.
Advise alcohol avoidance and hepatitis A vaccination if non-immune.

sections.title: Coinfections and India note
items: HIV coinfection: treat both with a tenofovir-containing antiretroviral regimen (TDF or TAF with lamivudine or emtricitabine); never leave lamivudine as the only HBV-active drug.
HDV coinfection (anti-HDV and HDV RNA positive): refer to hepatology; nucleos(t)ide analogues do not suppress HDV.
India's National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme provides free testing and antiviral drugs; its eligibility criteria may differ from WHO 2024, so check programme guidance for enrolment.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Using a single normal ALT or the older ALT limit of 40 U/L to deny treatment.
Forgetting HDV testing, and stopping therapy in a patient with cirrhosis (risk of fatal flare).
Starting rituximab or chemotherapy without HBV screening and prophylaxis.
Not dose-adjusting TDF or ETV to creatinine clearance.

drugs.name: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)
drugs.notes: CrCl 30 to 49: 300 mg every 48 hours; 10 to 29: every 72 to 96 hours; haemodialysis: every 7 days after dialysis. Monitor renal function.

drugs.name: Entecavir
drugs.dose: 0.5 mg orally once daily on an empty stomach; 1 mg once daily in decompensated liver disease
drugs.notes: CrCl 30 to 49: 0.25 mg daily; 10 to 29: 0.15 mg daily; below 10 or dialysis: 0.05 mg daily (oral solution) or equivalent interval extension. Not for lamivudine-resistant HBV.

drugs.name: Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF)
drugs.dose: 25 mg orally once daily with food
drugs.notes: Preferred with osteoporosis or renal impairment; no adjustment if CrCl 15 mL/min or more; not recommended below 15 unless on haemodialysis.

drugs.name: Tenofovir disoproxil (pregnancy prophylaxis)
drugs.dose: 300 mg orally once daily from the second trimester (by 28 weeks) until at least delivery
drugs.notes: HBV DNA 200,000 IU/mL or more, HBeAg positive, or all HBsAg-positive women where testing is unavailable.
